title: Basic Hydraulics for Water and Wastewater Operators
audience: Operators and trainees across the US and Canada preparing for certification exams and renewal in water and wastewater work.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic, a calculator and familiarity with pipes, pumps and tanks. US customary units are primary with metric equivalents; all scenarios and facility data are fictional.
introduction: Build the hydraulic arithmetic every operator uses: convert pressure to head, move among flow units, find velocity from pipe size, add up pump head, and calculate tank levels. Each module ends with worked examples that name the usual mistakes.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Pressure and head
objectives: Distinguish static, dynamic and residual pressure and convert between psi and feet of head.
Explain gauge versus absolute pressure and pressure at depth.
modules.lesson: ### Start with what the gauge is telling you Exam questions and real troubleshooting both depend on knowing *which* pressure you are looking at. Pressure is force per unit area, and in water systems it is almost always reported in pounds per square inch (psi). The metric equivalent is the kilopascal (kPa): 1 psi = 6.895 kPa. > **Your job:** connect every pressure reading to a water height, so that a gauge, a tank level and a hydraulic profile can all be compared on one scale. ### Static, dynamic and residual pressure **Static pressure** is the pressure in a pipe or tank when water is not moving. Open a hydrant on a quiet night with no flow and the gauge on the cap shows static pressure. In a gravity system fed from a tank or reservoir open to the air, it depends only on the height of the water surface above that point. **Dynamic pressure** (also called flowing or operating pressure) is the pressure at a point while water is flowing. With the same supply conditions it is lower than static pressure at the same point, because friction in pipe, fittings and valves uses up some head. (Engineering texts use "dynamic pressure" for a different quantity, velocity pressure; in operator work it means flowing pressure.) **Residual pressure** is the pressure that remains at a point while a stated flow is being drawn elsewhere. You meet it in hydrant flow tests: read static pressure at one hydrant, open another to flow, and read the residual pressure at the first. The difference between static and residual tells you how hard the system is working at that flow. A large drop at a modest test flow often points to a long or restricted supply path or limited supply capacity. | Term | When it is read | What it tells you | | --- | --- | --- | | Static | No flow | Height of water above the gauge | | Dynamic | While water flows | Pressure left after losses at that moment | | Residual | While a stated flow is drawn nearby | Margin that remains for customers or fire flow | ### Fluid at rest and fluid in motion **Hydrostatics** is the study of fluid at rest. Pressure in a standing fluid comes from the depth of fluid above the point. Operator example: a standpipe on a quiet night with every demand shut off. Its base gauge holds steady at a value set by depth, so 25 ft of water reads about 10.8 psi whatever the tank's width. **Hydrodynamics** is the study of fluid in motion. Moving water has speed as well as pressure, and friction takes head along the way. Operator example: a main feeding a neighbourhood at the morning peak, where the same gauge reads lower than it did at midnight because water is flowing. Static pressure is the hydrostatic case; dynamic and residual pressure belong to hydrodynamics, as do most of the ideas in Modules 2 to 4. ### The two constants you must know Fresh water weighs about 62.4 pounds per cubic foot. A column of water one foot tall and one square inch in cross-section therefore exerts a fixed pressure at its base. Rounded for operator use: - **0.433 psi per foot of water depth** (metric: 9.79 kPa per metre) - **2.31 feet of water per psi** (metric: 0.102 m per kPa, or about 0.704 m per psi) These are two forms of the same fact. 0.433 multiplied by 2.31 is very nearly 1. Use them like this: **psi = feet of water x 0.433** **feet of water = psi x 2.31** The quick sense-check is direction. Feet are a bigger number than psi (about 2.3 times bigger), so converting psi to feet should make the number larger, and converting feet to psi should make it smaller. If your answer moves the wrong way, you used the wrong constant. ### Head: pressure expressed as height Operators call a height of water **head**. Ignoring friction, a pump that adds 120 ft of head can lift water 120 ft, or push against a pressure of 120 x 0.433 = 52.0 psi. Head is useful because elevation, pressure and the energy added by a pump can all be added and subtracted in the same unit, feet. The pressure at a point in a tank depends on the **depth of water above that point**, not on the tank's width, shape or total volume. A narrow standpipe and a wide reservoir, each holding water 40 ft above the same gauge, give the same reading. This is why elevated tanks are built high rather than wide when the goal is pressure. ### Gauge versus absolute pressure (concept level) Most gauges read zero when open to the air. That reading is **gauge pressure**, written psig. **Absolute pressure** is measured from a perfect vacuum, so it equals gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure. At sea level atmospheric pressure is about 14.7 psi (101.3 kPa). For nearly all distribution work you use gauge pressure. Absolute pressure matters on the suction side of a pump, where the water can be pulled down toward the pressure at which it begins to vaporise. A suction gauge reading below zero means the absolute pressure is less than atmospheric. ### Worked example: tank, hydrant and pump *The Larkspur Hollow system is fictional. Use 0.433 psi per ft and 2.31 ft per psi.* **Part A: pressure at depth.** The water surface in the Larkspur Hollow elevated tank is 54 ft above a hydrant gauge. Static pressure at the gauge: 54 ft x 0.433 psi/ft = **23.4 psi** **Part B: head from pressure.** A booster pump at Larkspur Hollow has a discharge gauge reading of 120 psi and a suction gauge reading of 8 psi, with both gauges at about the same height. The pressure the pump adds is 120 minus 8 = 112 psi. As head: 112 psi x 2.31 ft/psi = **258.7 ft** Notice that the pump's contribution is the *difference* between the two gauges, not the discharge reading alone. A common error is to convert the discharge gauge only, which credits the pump with energy the incoming water already carried. **Part C: a flow test.** Static pressure at test hydrant 1 is 70 psi. With hydrant 2 flowing, residual pressure at hydrant 1 is 52 psi. The drop is 70 minus 52 = 18 psi, which is 18 x 2.31 = **41.6 ft** of head consumed by the flow. ### Using head to compare two gauges at different elevations Two connected points in a pipe that is not flowing share the same water surface level, so their pressures differ by the elevation difference. If a gauge sits 30 ft lower than another, it reads 30 x 0.433 = 13.0 psi higher. Moving down the hill adds pressure; moving up subtracts it. This is why customers at the bottom of a pressure zone see high pressure and those at the top see low pressure, even with no flow at all. When water is flowing, you also subtract the head lost to friction between the two points. That is the subject of Module 3. ### Common mistakes to watch for - **Wrong direction.** Multiplying psi by 0.433 or feet by 2.31 gives a number that looks plausible but moves the wrong way. Always check the direction. - **Reading discharge alone.** Pump head comes from the pressure difference between discharge and suction, not the discharge gauge by itself. - **Mixing gauge and absolute.** A "35 psi" gauge reading is about 49.7 psi absolute at sea level. Use absolute only when the question says so. - **Unit slips.** Keep psi, feet and kPa labelled in every line of your work. ### Before you move on You should now be able to separate hydrostatic from hydrodynamic situations, state what static, dynamic and residual pressure mean, convert between psi and feet of head, and explain why only depth sets pressure at a tank base. Module 2 moves from pressure to flow.

### Fictional scenario: the Larkspur Hollow pressure complaint

Larkspur Hollow is a fictional village. The operator reads a hydrant gauge at the base of the elevated tank on a quiet night: **65 psi static**. At the top of a hill 90 ft above that gauge, a customer reports weak pressure. During a flow test a hydrant on the hill is opened, and the pressure at the base hydrant falls from 65 to 49 psi.

### Your decision

Convert each number to feet of head with 2.31 ft per psi and 0.433 psi per ft. State which readings are static and which are residual. Estimate the static pressure on the hill and explain why the flowing reading is lower.
modules.assignment: Prepare a one-page gauge log for the Larkspur Hollow readings. For each reading label it as static or residual, convert it between psi and feet, and compute the expected static pressure 90 ft higher. Explain in two sentences why residual is lower than static.
rubric: Labels static and residual readings correctly.
Uses 2.31 ft per psi and 0.433 psi per ft in the right direction.
Subtracts elevation gain when moving uphill.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Base static 65 psi = 150.2 ft. Residual 49 psi = 113.2 ft; drop 16 psi = 37.0 ft. Hill static is 65 - 90 x 0.433 = 26.0 psi. Residual is lower because friction takes head while water flows. Do not accept a direction error in either conversion.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator reads a hydrant cap gauge on a quiet night with no demand anywhere on the zone. The reading is best described as:
choices: Dynamic pressure, set by the pump running at full flow
Residual pressure, set by the flow drawn at a nearby hydrant
Static pressure, set by the height of water above the gauge
Absolute pressure, set from a perfect vacuum upward
checks.explanation: With no flow, the gauge shows static pressure, which depends only on the height of water above it. The "Dynamic pressure, set by the pump running at full flow" choice confuses static with dynamic pressure, which is read only while water moves. The "Residual pressure, set by the flow drawn at a nearby hydrant" choice confuses static with residual pressure, which needs a stated flow elsewhere. The "Absolute pressure, set from a perfect vacuum upward" choice mixes up the zero reference, because a cap gauge reads gauge pressure.

checks.prompt: A fictional standpipe holds water 40 ft deep above a gauge at its base. Using 0.433 psi per ft (9.79 kPa per m), the gauge pressure is:
checks.explanation: 40 x 0.433 = 17.32 psi, about 17.3 psi. The "92.4 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31, the feet-per-psi constant, which is the wrong direction for converting feet to psi. The "32.0 psi" choice added atmospheric pressure to a gauge reading, which converts it to absolute pressure. The "0.011 psi" choice divided the constant by the depth instead of multiplying depth by the constant.

checks.prompt: A fictional booster pump raises water pressure by 52 psi. Using 2.31 ft of head per psi (0.704 m per psi), the head added is:
checks.explanation: 52 x 2.31 = 120.1 ft of head. The "22.5 ft" choice multiplied by 0.433, which converts feet to psi, so psi was treated as feet. The "358.5 ft" choice multiplied by 6.895, the psi-to-kPa constant, and labelled the answer feet. The "54.3 ft" choice added the constant instead of multiplying by it.

checks.prompt: A fictional gauge on a sea-level main reads 60 psi (gauge). Taking atmospheric pressure as 14.7 psi (101.3 kPa), the absolute pressure is:
checks.explanation: Absolute equals gauge plus atmospheric: 60 + 14.7 = 74.7 psi. The "45.3 psi" choice subtracted atmospheric pressure, which moves from absolute toward gauge instead of from gauge to absolute. The "60.0 psi" choice treated the gauge reading as absolute and ignored atmospheric pressure. The "882.0 psi" choice multiplied by atmospheric pressure instead of adding it.

checks.prompt: During a fictional hydrant flow test, the pressure read at the observation hydrant while another hydrant is flowing is called the:
choices: Static pressure, the pressure measured with the system at rest
Absolute pressure, the pressure measured from a vacuum reference
Residual pressure, the pressure remaining while the stated flow is drawn
Shutoff pressure, the pressure a pump makes at zero flow
checks.explanation: Residual pressure is what remains at the observation point while the test flow is drawn, and the drop from static shows how hard the system is working. The "Static pressure, the pressure measured with the system at rest" choice confuses residual with static, which is read before the flow starts. The "Absolute pressure, the pressure measured from a vacuum reference" choice confuses residual with absolute, which only changes the zero point. The "Shutoff pressure, the pressure a pump makes at zero flow" choice names a pump characteristic at zero flow, not a reading taken at an observation hydrant while the test flow runs.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator reads the pressure at the base of a standing tank with no draw, then at a main that is carrying flow. Which pairing of terms is correct?
choices: Tank base is hydrostatic (fluid at rest); flowing main is hydrodynamic (fluid in motion)
Tank base is hydrodynamic (fluid in motion); flowing main is hydrostatic (fluid at rest)
Tank base and flowing main are hydrostatic, since each holds water under pressure
Tank base is hydrostatic because it is large; flowing main is hydrodynamic because it is buried
checks.explanation: Water at rest is the hydrostatic case and water in motion is the hydrodynamic case, so the tank base is hydrostatic and the flowing main is hydrodynamic. The "Tank base is hydrodynamic (fluid in motion); flowing main is hydrostatic (fluid at rest)" choice swaps the two terms. The "Tank base and flowing main are hydrostatic, since each holds water under pressure" choice ignores motion, which is what separates the two ideas. The "Tank base is hydrostatic because it is large; flowing main is hydrodynamic because it is buried" choice sorts by size and location, which have nothing to do with whether the fluid moves.

modules.title: Flow, area and velocity
objectives: Apply Q = A x V and continuity to circular pipes and rectangular channels.
Convert among gpm, cfs and MGD and predict velocity changes with pipe size.
modules.lesson: ### Start with the question the flow meter answers A flow meter answers one question: how much water passes a point per unit time? Operators then need to translate that number into pipe velocity, tank filling time or plant throughput, and across the US and Canada the same flow is quoted in several units. This module gives you one relationship, **Q = A x V**, and a short list of conversions that cover almost every exam problem. > **Your job:** keep the units consistent. Most wrong answers in flow problems come from mixing feet, inches, gallons and minutes in one line of arithmetic. ### The flow equation For water filling a pipe or channel, the flow rate equals the cross-sectional area of the flowing water multiplied by its average velocity: **Q = A x V** - Q is flow in cubic feet per second (cfs) when A is in square feet and V is in feet per second (ft/s). - A is the area at right angles to the direction of flow. - V is the average velocity. (1 ft/s = 0.305 m/s.) Rearranged, **V = Q / A** and **A = Q / V**. Because A sits in the denominator of the velocity equation, the same flow moves *faster* through a smaller area. That single fact explains why a partly closed valve jets water, why a small service line is noisy, and why velocity rises in a reducer. ### Areas you need **Circular pipe** flowing full: **A = pi x d squared / 4**, or equivalently pi x r squared, where r is the radius, half the diameter. Diameters are quoted in inches but the equation needs feet, so divide by 12 first. (1 in = 25.4 mm.) For an 8 in pipe, d = 8 / 12 = 0.667 ft and A = 3.1416 x 0.667 squared / 4 = **0.349 square feet**. Two classic errors: using the diameter where the formula wants the radius, which overstates area four-fold, and forgetting to square. **Rectangular channel**: **A = width x depth of water** Use the depth of the *water*, not the depth of the channel wall. A 3 ft wide channel with water 1.5 ft deep has A = 4.5 square feet. ### The conversions Operators move between four common flow units. Learn the constants and what each one links. Gallons in this course are US gallons (an Imperial gallon is about 1.2 US gallons). | Constant | Meaning | Metric equivalent | | --- | --- | --- | | 7.48 gal per cubic foot | volume | 1 ft3 = 28.3 L | | 449 gpm per cfs | flow, gallons per minute and cubic feet per second | 1 cfs = 28.3 L/s; 1 gpm = 0.0631 L/s | | 1.547 cfs per MGD | flow, million gallons per day and cfs | 1 MGD = 43.8 L/s | | 694.4 gpm per MGD | 1,000,000 gal per day divided by 1,440 min per day | 1 MGD = 43.8 L/s | Where do they come from? 1 cfs is 7.48 gal each second, and there are 60 seconds in a minute, so 7.48 x 60 = 448.8, rounded to 449 gpm. One MGD is 1,000,000 gal per day, which is 1,000,000 / 1,440 = 694.4 gpm, and 694.4 / 449 = 1.547 cfs. Knowing the derivation helps you rebuild a constant if you forget one. The sense-check for direction: a cfs is a large unit (449 gpm), so converting gpm to cfs makes the number smaller, and converting cfs to gpm makes it bigger. MGD to gpm makes the number much bigger. ### Continuity: the same flow, different pipe sizes For steady flow with nothing added or removed, the flow is the same at every section of a pipe. So **Q = A1 x V1 = A2 x V2** and therefore **V2 = V1 x (A1 / A2)**. Because area depends on the *square* of the diameter, halving a pipe's diameter makes the area one-quarter and the velocity four times higher. Doubling the diameter drops the velocity to one-quarter. Velocity does not change in proportion to diameter; it changes inversely with the square of the diameter: V2 = V1 x (d1 / d2) squared. That is the most tested continuity idea. Higher velocity matters for operations: friction losses climb (Module 3), surge pressures from a sudden stop are larger (Module 4), and scour or noise can develop in fittings. ### Worked example: a transfer main with a reducer *The Brightwater Bluffs booster station is fictional. Use 7.48 gal per ft3, 449 gpm per cfs.* A 10 in main carries 700 gpm and then narrows to a 6 in line. **Step 1: convert the flow to cfs.** 700 gpm / 449 gpm per cfs = **1.559 cfs**. **Step 2: area of the 10 in main.** d = 10 / 12 = 0.8333 ft. A = 3.1416 x 0.8333 squared / 4 = **0.5454 ft2**. **Step 3: velocity in the 10 in main.** V = Q / A = 1.559 / 0.5454 = **2.86 ft/s** (0.87 m/s). **Step 4: area of the 6 in line.** d = 0.5 ft, A = 3.1416 x 0.5 squared / 4 = **0.1963 ft2**. **Step 5: velocity in the 6 in line.** V = 1.559 / 0.1963 = **7.94 ft/s** (2.42 m/s). **Sense-check by ratio.** The area ratio is (10 / 6) squared = 2.78, and 2.86 x 2.78 = 7.95 ft/s, which matches 7.94 ft/s within rounding. The calculation agrees. Notice that the diameter ratio alone (1.67) would have given only 4.8 ft/s, which is the typical shortcut error. ### A second example: from MGD to channel velocity A plant effluent channel is 4 ft wide with water 2 ft deep. The plant is passing 3.0 MGD. Convert: 3.0 MGD x 1.547 = 4.64 cfs. Area = 4 x 2 = 8 ft2. Velocity = 4.64 / 8 = **0.58 ft/s**. A low velocity such as this is typical of a settling or effluent channel. If the same flow were forced through a half-depth channel the velocity would double, because the area halved. ### Common mistakes to watch for - **Diameter in inches in the area formula.** Convert to feet first, or your area will be in square inches and 144 times too large when mixed with cfs. - **Radius versus diameter.** Check which one the formula wants. Pi x d squared / 4 uses diameter; pi x r squared uses radius. - **Forgetting to convert gpm to cfs.** If the answer is in the thousands of ft/s, a conversion step was skipped. - **Dividing when you should multiply.** Remember cfs are bigger units than gpm. Use the direction check. - **Comparing diameters rather than areas.** Velocity scales with the square of the diameter ratio (larger pipe, slower water). - **Using channel depth rather than water depth.** Area is the wetted section only. ### Before you move on You should now be able to compute the area of a circular pipe or rectangular channel, apply Q = A x V in either direction, convert among gpm, cfs and MGD using 449, 7.48 and 1.547, and predict qualitatively how velocity changes when pipe size changes. Module 3 asks what that velocity costs in energy.

modules.title: Friction, energy and pumps
objectives: Identify what drives friction loss and interpret the Hazen-Williams C factor.
Build a total dynamic head, calculate water and brake horsepower and recognise operating point shifts.
modules.lesson: ### Start with energy, not just pressure Water in a pipe carries energy as height, pressure and motion. A pump adds energy and friction removes it. Module 1 wrote pressure and elevation as head in feet, and this module keeps that currency. > **Your job:** say where the energy goes between the pump and the customer, and what changes when that path changes. ### What drives friction loss Rubbing against the pipe wall and turbulence turn some energy into heat. That energy leaves the hydraulic system as **friction head loss**, in feet. Four things drive it: **flow** (loss rises faster than flow, roughly with its 1.85 power), **diameter** (smaller pipe means higher velocity and much more loss), **length** (loss is proportional to length) and **roughness**. Fittings, valves and strainers add **minor losses**. In the Hazen-Williams equation the roughness coefficient **C** works backward from what the word suggests: a **higher C** is a **smoother** pipe with **less** loss, and a **lower C** is a rougher, older pipe with more loss. C falls as pipe ages, so a pump that suited a new main can fall short years later. ### Static suction head and static discharge head Both are vertical distances measured from the **pump centerline**, the shaft axis, and both are measured at rest, so neither includes friction. - **Static suction head** is the vertical distance from the centerline up to the liquid surface on the supply side, when the supply sits above the pump (a flooded suction). If the supply sits below the pump, the same distance is a **static suction lift**. - **Static discharge head** is the vertical distance from the centerline up to the liquid surface, or the free discharge point, on the delivery side. **Static head = static discharge head - static suction head**, and with a lift you add the lift instead. Fictional Otter Run example: the delivery tank surface is 42 ft above the centerline. With the wet-well surface 5 ft below it (a lift), static head = 42 + 5 = **47 ft**. With a supply surface 5 ft above it (suction head), static head = 42 - 5 = **37 ft**. Using the discharge head alone ignores the supply side. ### Total dynamic head: static, friction and velocity The head a pump must supply is its **total dynamic head (TDH)**: **TDH = static head + friction head + velocity head** - **Static head** is the net of the static discharge and suction heads above, the elevation difference between the supply and delivery surfaces. - **Friction head** includes pipe and minor losses at the pumped flow. - **Velocity head** is the energy of motion written as a height: **V squared / (2 x g)**, with V in ft/s and g = 32.2 ft/s squared (9.81 m/s squared). At 2 to 8 ft/s it runs from about 0.06 to 1 ft: small, but include it when a velocity is given. If the pump delivers into a pressurised tank, add the required pressure head, converting psi to feet with 2.31 ft per psi. **Worked example (fictional Marsh Landing pump).** Static head 52 ft. Friction head at the pumped flow 14 ft. Discharge velocity 6 ft/s. Velocity head = 6 squared / 64.4 = 36 / 64.4 = **0.56 ft**. TDH = 52 + 14 + 0.56 = **66.56 ft**, about 66.6 ft (20.3 m). Because friction and velocity both depend on flow, TDH is not one number; it changes with the flow being pumped. ### Net positive suction head, conceptually A pump can fail on the *suction* side even when its discharge side is fine. **Net positive suction head available (NPSHa)** is how much energy the water has at the suction, above the point where it would begin to vaporise. It grows with atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi, about 34 ft of water at sea level; 101.3 kPa) and with water standing above the pump, and it shrinks with suction lift, suction-line friction and warmer water, which vaporises more easily. **NPSH required (NPSHr)** is a property of the pump, published by the manufacturer, and it generally rises as flow increases. The rule is plain: **NPSHa must be at least NPSHr**, with a safety margin. When it is not, vapour bubbles form at the impeller and the pump cavitates (Module 4). Raising the wet-well level or shortening the suction line raises NPSHa; higher flow raises NPSHr. ### Pump curve and operating point On a typical centrifugal pump curve the highest head comes at zero flow, the **shutoff head**; as flow rises, head falls. Always check the manufacturer's curve for the actual shape. Plot the system's required head on the same axes. The **operating point** is where the curves cross. Throttle a valve, raise the tank level or let the pipe get rougher, and the system curve steepens or rises, so the point moves to lower flow. Impeller wear lowers the pump curve instead. When flow disappoints, ask which curve moved. ### Affinity laws: changing pump speed For the same pump and impeller, changing speed N (rpm) scales performance in a fixed pattern: - **Flow** varies with speed: Q2 = Q1 x (N2 / N1) - **Head** varies with speed squared: H2 = H1 x (N2 / N1) squared - **Power** varies with speed cubed: P2 = P1 x (N2 / N1) cubed **Worked example (fictional Pine Terrace pump).** At 1,750 rpm the pump delivers 1,200 gpm at 80 ft and draws 30 BHP. A variable-speed drive lowers it to 1,400 rpm, a ratio of 0.80. Flow: 1,200 x 0.80 = **960 gpm**. Head: 80 x 0.80 squared = 80 x 0.64 = **51.2 ft**. Power: 30 x 0.80 cubed = 30 x 0.512 = **15.4 BHP**. **Calculation check.** A 20 percent speed cut gives 20 percent less flow but nearly half the power (0.512), which is why speed control saves energy. If your power fell only 20 percent, you applied the flow law to power. With a large static head, actual flow falls more than the flow law suggests, so check the new crossing with the system curve. ### Water horsepower and brake horsepower: keep them separate **Water horsepower (WHP)** is the power delivered to the water: **WHP = Q x H / 3,960**, with Q in gpm and H in ft. **Brake horsepower (BHP)** is the power the pump shaft must receive: **BHP = WHP / pump efficiency**, with efficiency as a decimal. WHP never includes efficiency; BHP always does, and BHP is the larger. Motor losses add a further step: **input hp = BHP / motor efficiency**. (1 hp = 0.746 kW.) ### Pumping energy and the cost of one extra foot **Worked example (fictional Heron Bay station).** Flow 1,000 gpm, TDH 90 ft, pump efficiency 70 percent, motor efficiency 92 percent, running 8,760 hours per year. WHP = 1,000 x 90 / 3,960 = **22.73 hp**. BHP = 22.73 / 0.70 = **32.47 hp**. Input = 32.47 / 0.92 = **35.29 hp**. In kW: 35.29 x 0.746 = **26.33 kW**. Energy: 26.33 x 8,760 = **230,624 kWh per year**. Power rises in proportion to head at fixed flow and efficiency, so one extra foot of lift costs 230,624 / 90 = **about 2,562 kWh per year**. At a fictional 10 cents per kWh that is about 256 dollars per year per foot. ### Common mistakes to watch for - **Leaving out a term of TDH,** or using discharge head alone as the static head. - **Treating NPSHa and NPSHr as the same thing;** one belongs to the system, the other to the pump. - **Applying one affinity law to all three quantities.** - **Mixing WHP and BHP,** or multiplying by efficiency. - **Forgetting 3,960** or labelling kW as hp. ### Before you move on You should be able to define static suction and discharge head, build TDH, state the NPSH rule, scale a pump with the affinity laws, keep WHP and BHP separate, and turn power into kWh per year. Module 4 uses these ideas on the plant floor.

Suction lift 52 ft; static discharge head 60 ft

Together they make 68 ft of static head for total dynamic head. The "Suction lift 60 ft; static discharge head 8 ft" choice swaps the two distances. The "Suction lift 8 ft; static discharge head 68 ft" choice adds the lift into the discharge head, which counts it twice once the lift is added again in TDH. checks.prompt: A fictional pump has an efficiency below 100 percent. Compared with water horsepower, the brake horsepower needed is:

Equal, because the water receives the full shaft power

Greater, because BHP equals WHP divided by efficiency
checks.explanation: BHP = WHP / efficiency, with efficiency as a decimal below one, so BHP is always larger than WHP. checks.prompt: A fictional pump is cavitating at its suction. For a pump to avoid this, the usual rule for net positive suction head is that:
choices: Available NPSH must be at least equal to the NPSH the pump requires
Required NPSH must be at least equal to the NPSH available
Available NPSH must equal the discharge head of the pump
Required NPSH must be zero whenever the water is cool
checks.explanation: NPSHa belongs to the system and NPSHr to the pump, and NPSHa must meet or exceed NPSHr, with a margin, or vapour forms at the impeller. The "Required NPSH must be at least equal to the NPSH available" choice reverses the rule, as if the pump set the supply and not the system. The "Available NPSH must equal the discharge head of the pump" choice mixes up a suction-side margin with total pump head. The "Required NPSH must be zero whenever the water is cool" choice treats a pump property as if it depended on water temperature alone.

modules.lesson: ### Start with the symptom Operators see low pressure, noise, vibration or a tank that will not fill, not a named cause. This module links symptoms to Modules 1 to 3 and teaches tank arithmetic. It is **recognition-level**: it helps you name what you see, and it does not replace your facility's procedures or your supervisor's direction. > **Your job:** match a pattern in pressure, flow, sound or power draw to its usual hydraulic cause, then calculate what you can. ### Pump types at recognition level A **kinetic pump** (an impeller or propeller) gives the liquid speed and turns that speed into pressure, so its flow falls as head rises along the pump curve. Jet eductors and airlifts also lift liquid without trapping a fixed volume, but they work by a fast jet or by lighter aerated liquid, not by an impeller. A **positive displacement pump** traps a fixed volume and pushes it out each turn or stroke, so flow stays steady as pressure changes and a closed discharge builds pressure until something relieves it. Positive displacement pumps need a relief device. | Pump | Purpose in one line | Suits | | --- | --- | --- | | Radial centrifugal (kinetic) | Impeller throws water outward; the common general-duty pump | Clear water, treated flow | | Mixed flow (kinetic) | Between radial and axial; more flow at lower head | Large clear-water flows | | Axial flow (kinetic) | Propeller pushes water along the shaft; very large flow, low head | Stormwater, recirculation | | Vortex or torque-flow (kinetic) | Recessed impeller swirls the liquid so solids pass by | Raw wastewater with rags | | Jet eductor (jet-driven) | A fast jet draws in and carries other liquid, no moving parts | Chemical solution feed, small lifts | | Airlift (air-driven) | Air in a riser makes the mix lighter so it rises | Gentle return sludge, scum | | Pneumatic ejector (air displacement) | Air pressure pushes batches out of a sealed pot | Small remote wastewater lift stations | | Screw (positive displacement) | Meshing screws carry liquid along the casing | Thick sludge, viscous liquids | | Progressing cavity (positive displacement) | Rotor turns inside a rubber stator, making moving pockets | Thick sludge, polymer | | Rotary lobe (positive displacement) | Two synchronized lobed rotors carry liquid in pockets between the rotors and the casing | Sludge, scum | | Gear (positive displacement) | Meshing gears trap liquid between teeth | Clean oils, not abrasive sludge | | Plunger (positive displacement) | Piston stroke makes high pressure at small flow | High-pressure small flows | | Diaphragm (positive displacement) | A flexing membrane gives an adjustable, steady stroke volume | Chemical metering | ### Cavitation: recognition Cavitation starts when pressure at the impeller eye falls so low that water vaporises. The bubbles then collapse hard as pressure rises inside the pump. Look for **noise** like gravel or crackling, **vibration**, pitting on the impeller and **falling flow and head**. Usual causes are too much suction lift, a plugged screen or suction valve, warm water, or running far off the design flow. This is the NPSH rule failing: available suction head is no longer safely above what the pump requires. ### Air binding Air in the casing or suction line makes a pump surge, gurgle or deliver little, often with lower motor current. Typical causes are leaking suction joints and a vortex at a low wet-well level. Air binding is air or gas gathered in the pump, often from leaks, a vortex or poor priming; cavitation is vapour formed from the water itself by low pressure. ### Priming and starting a centrifugal pump: recognition only A centrifugal pump moves liquid, not air. Its impeller builds suction and pressure only when the casing and suction line are full of liquid; with air inside, it spins and delivers little or nothing. **Priming** is filling the casing and suction line with liquid. A pump above its supply may have a **foot valve**, a check valve at the foot of the suction pipe that holds liquid in place, or a **priming system** that draws liquid up with vacuum. A pump with the supply above its centerline fills by gravity and usually needs neither. **Dry running** is operating without liquid. The pumped liquid cools and lubricates the seals, so a dry pump can overheat and damage them quickly. **Discharge valve position at start** matters because a radial centrifugal pump draws the least power near zero flow, while an axial pump is the reverse. Whether to start against a closed, partly open or open valve, and how fast to open it, is set by the manufacturer and the facility. **A pump that has lost prime** shows little or no flow, discharge pressure near zero or swinging, lower motor current, and gurgling at the suction. Compare cavitation (gravel noise, vibration) and a closed discharge valve (high pressure near shutoff). This course teaches recognition, not start-up steps. Facility procedures, manufacturer instructions and lockout rules govern. ### Water hammer If velocity changes quickly, the moving water's momentum becomes pressure waves that can spike pressure upward or drop it low. Triggers include fast valve closure, a sudden pump stop or a slamming check valve. Risk grows with higher velocity, longer pipe and faster change. No single closing time suits every pipe; the right rate comes from your system's own data. ### Cause-to-symptom table for common pump problems | Symptom | Common causes | | --- | --- | | Low flow | Worn impeller, partly closed or blocked valve, air in suction, rougher pipe, speed too low | | Low pressure | Large demand or break downstream, worn impeller, low speed, air binding | | High power draw | Running far out on the curve at high flow, binding or misaligned parts, clogged impeller, tight packing | Use the table to form a question, then confirm with instruments and your maintenance staff. ### Valve types, including wastewater valves | Valve | Purpose and typical use | | --- | --- | | Gate | Isolation; fully open or fully closed, low loss when open | | Globe | Throttling and flow control; high loss even when open | | Ball | Quick isolation or on and off; low loss, quarter turn | | Butterfly | Isolation and moderate throttling in large lines; disc stays in the flow | | Check | One-way flow; stops reverse flow at a pump discharge | | Plug | Isolation or switching in gas, sludge and slurry lines; quarter turn | | Knife gate | Isolation in thick sludge or solids; the blade cuts through | | Pinch | Throttling and isolation of slurries and powders; a flexible sleeve squeezes shut | | Mud | Valve, often a gate or plug valve, at a tank or basin floor that drains settled sludge by gravity | | Telescoping | Sliding pipe sleeve, raised or lowered to set the level at which liquid is drawn off a tank | **Throttling versus isolation.** An isolation valve should be fully open or fully closed. Holding a gate valve partly open to control flow can damage the gate and seat. A valve intended for throttling, such as a globe, is built to sit part open, and in a typical centrifugal-pump system every throttled valve adds head loss that raises pressure upstream and cuts flow. ### Reading a pressure and flow trend Flow up with pressure down suggests a bigger draw such as a break or open hydrant. Flow down with pressure up suggests a restriction downstream of the gauge. Both falling points to supply, such as pump wear or suction trouble. Treat a pattern as a hint, not a diagnosis. ### Tank level, fill and drain Volume per foot of depth is area x 1 ft, and A = pi x d squared / 4 with d in feet. Convert ft3 to gallons with 7.48 gal per ft3 (1 ft3 = 28.3 L). Net flow is inflow minus outflow, and the level changes at net ft3/min divided by tank area. **Worked example (fictional Willow Gap tank).** The tank is 36 ft in diameter. Pumps supply 600 gpm and customers draw 850 gpm. Net flow = 600 - 850 = **-250 gpm**. Area = 3.1416 x 36 squared / 4 = **1,017.9 ft2**. Net outflow in ft3/min = 250 / 7.48 = **33.42**. Rate = 33.42 / 1,017.9 = 0.03283 ft/min, or x 60 = **1.97 ft per hour**. Time to fall 5 ft = 5 / 1.97 = **2.54 hours**. ### Common mistakes to watch for - Forgetting 7.48, or using diameter as radius in the tank area. - Using inflow or outflow alone instead of the difference. - Holding an isolation-only valve, such as a gate valve, partly open to throttle flow. ### Before you move on You should be able to name common kinetic and positive displacement pumps, explain priming and dry running at recognition level, recognise cavitation, air binding and water hammer, pick valves including mud and telescoping valves, and calculate tank levels.

checks.prompt: In a fictional transmission main, a large pressure spike with banging in the pipe follows a quick valve closure. This pattern is recognised as:
choices: Cavitation, caused by vapour forming at the impeller
Air binding, caused by air trapped in the pump casing
Dead-end loss, caused by one path feeding a customer
Water hammer, caused by a rapid change in water velocity
checks.explanation: Fast changes in velocity convert the moving water's momentum to a pressure spike, which is water hammer. The "Cavitation, caused by vapour forming at the impeller" choice confuses a pipeline surge with a pump suction problem. The "Air binding, caused by air trapped in the pump casing" choice confuses a pipeline surge with an air problem inside a pump. The "Dead-end loss, caused by one path feeding a customer" choice confuses a sudden event with a steady low-pressure pattern.

checks.prompt: A fictional pump runs with lower-than-normal motor current, a gurgling suction and a surging discharge gauge. The most likely cause is:
choices: A discharge valve closed fast enough to cause surge
A pump impeller pitted by long-running cavitation damage
A long dead-end main creating friction at peak demand
Air entering or trapped in the suction side of the pump
checks.explanation: Gurgling, surging pressure and low amps are typical signs of air in the suction, known as air binding. The "A discharge valve closed fast enough to cause surge" choice links a sustained surging gauge with a one-time valve event. The "A pump impeller pitted by long-running cavitation damage" choice assumes damage from a past problem explains the low current right now. The "A long dead-end main creating friction at peak demand" choice links a suction symptom with a distribution layout.

checks.prompt: A fictional pump makes a crackling noise like gravel, vibrates, and pits its impeller. Suction pressure at the pump is very low. This pattern is recognised as:
choices: Water hammer, where a rapid velocity change makes a spike
Air binding, where air blocks the casing and flow stops
Cavitation, where low pressure lets water vaporise at the impeller
Throttling, where a partly closed valve raises pressure
checks.explanation: Gravel-like noise, vibration and impeller pitting at very low suction pressure indicate cavitation. The "Water hammer, where a rapid velocity change makes a spike" choice confuses gravel-like noise with banging in the pipeline. The "Air binding, where air blocks the casing and flow stops" choice confuses vapour that formed from low pressure with trapped air or gas. The "Throttling, where a partly closed valve raises pressure" choice names a valve action, not the pattern; a restricted suction valve can cause cavitation, but the noise, pitting and low suction pressure identify cavitation itself.

checks.prompt: A fictional operator asks why a centrifugal pump must be filled with liquid before it runs. Which reason is correct?
choices: The casing needs the weight of water to sit steady during start-up
An impeller turning in air builds little suction, and dry running overheats seals
Water in the casing lets the motor reach full speed sooner
A full casing keeps the discharge check valve seated during start-up
checks.explanation: A centrifugal impeller works on liquid, not air, so a dry pump cannot draw liquid up, and the liquid at the shaft seal also cools and lubricates it, so a dry pump can quickly overheat and damage the seal. The "casing needs the weight of water" choice treats priming as a stability issue, which it is not. The "lets the motor reach full speed sooner" choice mixes up motor speed with the pump's ability to build suction. The "keeps the discharge check valve seated" choice links priming to a valve that is a separate part with its own job.

checks.prompt: A fictional cylindrical tank is 40 ft in diameter. Pumps supply 800 gpm while customers draw 500 gpm. Using 7.48 gal per ft3, the level changes by about:
checks.explanation: Net = 300 gpm. Area = 1256.6 ft2. 300/7.48 = 40.11 ft3/min, so 0.0319 ft/min, or 1.91 ft per hour. The "Rises 0.03 ft per hour" choice forgot to multiply the per-minute rate by 60 to get per hour. The "Rises 0.48 ft per hour" choice used the diameter as the radius when finding tank area. The "Rises 5.1 ft per hour" choice used the inflow alone instead of the net flow.

checks.prompt: A fictional plant must feed a small, steady chemical dose even as discharge pressure changes. Which pump type suits the job?
choices: Radial centrifugal pump, whose flow stays steady as pressure changes
Diaphragm pump, a positive displacement type with a set volume per stroke
Axial flow pump, built for large flows at low head
Airlift, which raises liquid with compressed air in a riser
checks.explanation: A diaphragm pump delivers a set volume each stroke, so flow stays near steady and can be adjusted, which suits metering. The "Radial centrifugal pump" choice has the facts reversed, because centrifugal flow falls as head rises. The "Axial flow pump" choice suits large, low-head flows, not small doses. The "Airlift" choice suits gentle lifting of sludge, not accurate dosing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional elevated tank has its water surface 185 ft above a hydrant gauge. Using 0.433 psi per ft (9.79 kPa per m) and no flow, the static pressure is:
finalAssessment.explanation: 185 x 0.433 = 80.11 psi, about 80.1 psi. The "427.4 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31, which is the feet-per-psi constant used in the wrong direction. The "94.8 psi" choice added 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure to a gauge reading. The "65.4 psi" choice subtracted 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure from a gauge reading, which is never needed for gauge pressure.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant sends 3.2 MGD through a 16 in pipe flowing full. Use 1.547 cfs per MGD (1 MGD = 43.8 L/s) and a pipe area of 1.396 ft2. The velocity is:
finalAssessment.explanation: 3.2 x 1.547 = 4.950 cfs and V = 4.950 / 1.396 = 3.55 ft/s. The "2.29 ft/s" choice skipped the MGD to cfs conversion before dividing by area. The "6.91 ft/s" choice multiplied flow by area instead of dividing flow by area. The "0.89 ft/s" choice used a diameter-as-radius area of 5.585 ft2 for the division.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump lifts water 38 ft from the wet well level to a tank overflow. Friction head is 14.5 ft and discharge velocity is 8 ft/s. Using velocity head = V squared / (2 x g) with g = 32.2 ft/s squared (9.81 m/s squared), the total dynamic head is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Velocity head = 8 squared / 64.4 = 0.994 ft, and TDH = 38 + 14.5 + 0.994 = 53.49 ft. The "52.5 ft" choice left out the velocity head. The "54.5 ft" choice divided V squared by g and forgot the factor of 2 in the velocity head. The "52.6 ft" choice forgot to square the velocity before dividing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional cylindrical tank is 30 ft in diameter with no inflow. Customers draw 350 gpm. Using 7.48 gal per ft3, the time for the level to fall 8 ft is about:
finalAssessment.explanation: Area = 706.9 ft2, volume = 5654.9 ft3 = 42,298 gal, and 42,298 / 350 = 120.9 min. The "16.2 minutes" choice forgot to convert cubic feet to gallons with 7.48. The "483.4 minutes" choice used the diameter as the radius when finding tank area. The "2.0 minutes" choice divided by 60 and kept the minutes label, which gives hours.

finalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional pressure zone with no flow, gauge A sits at elevation 540 ft and reads 52 psi. Gauge B is on the same connected main at elevation 480 ft. Using 2.31 ft per psi, the static pressure at gauge B is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Gauge A holds 120.1 ft of head, so the water surface is 660.1 ft elevation. At gauge B the head is 180.1 ft, which is 77.97 psi. Equivalently 52 + 60 x 0.433 = 77.98 psi. The "26.0 psi" choice subtracted the elevation difference, which is the wrong direction because gauge B is lower and reads higher. The "112.0 psi" choice added 60 ft of elevation directly to psi without converting feet to psi. The "52.0 psi" choice assumed both gauges read alike, ignoring the 60 ft elevation difference.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional cylindrical tank is 20 ft in diameter and holds water 12 ft deep. Using 7.48 gal per ft3 (1 ft3 = 28.3 L), the volume in gallons is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Area = pi x 20 squared / 4 = 314.2 ft2, volume = 3769.9 ft3, and x 7.48 = 28,199 gal. The "112,796 gal" choice used the diameter in place of the radius, overstating area four-fold. The "3,770 gal" choice left the volume in cubic feet and never applied 7.48. The "504 gal" choice divided by 7.48 instead of multiplying.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump delivers 1,200 gpm at 75 ft of total head with an efficiency of 80 percent. Using WHP = Q x H / 3,960 and BHP = WHP / efficiency, the brake horsepower is:
finalAssessment.explanation: WHP = 1200 x 75 / 3,960 = 22.73 hp and BHP = 22.73 / 0.8 = 28.41 hp. The "18.2 hp" choice multiplied water horsepower by efficiency instead of dividing. The "22.7 hp" choice stopped at water horsepower and left out the efficiency. The "112,500 hp" choice divided by efficiency but forgot to divide by 3,960.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional trend shows discharge pressure sliding from 62 psi to 48 psi over two hours while the metered flow rises. The pattern most often indicates:
choices: A large uncontrolled draw downstream, such as a break or open hydrant
A partly closed valve that is restricting the line downstream
Air trapped in the pump casing so little water is moved
A tank filling and raising the pressure at the pump
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow up with pressure down means friction rises with a larger draw, so look for a break, an open hydrant or heavy demand. The "A partly closed valve that is restricting the line downstream" choice would cut flow while raising pressure, the opposite of this trend. The "Air trapped in the pump casing so little water is moved" choice would reduce flow, but the meter shows more flow. The "A tank filling and raising the pressure at the pump" choice would raise pressure, but the trend shows it falling.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump has a discharge gauge reading of 88 psi and a suction gauge reading of 6 psi, with both gauges at the same height. Using 2.31 ft per psi, the head the pump adds is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Pressure added is 88 - 6 = 82 psi, and 82 x 2.31 = 189.4 ft. The "203.3 ft" choice converted the discharge gauge alone, which credits the pump with energy already in the suction water. The "82.0 ft" choice left the answer in psi and labelled it feet, with no conversion by 2.31. The "35.5 ft" choice multiplied by 0.433, the feet-to-psi constant, in the wrong direction.

finalAssessment.prompt: Constant flow passes from a fictional 24 in main into a 12 in main. Velocity in the 24 in main is 1.8 ft/s. Velocity in the 12 in main is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Area falls to one-quarter, so velocity rises by 4: 1.8 x 4 = 7.2 ft/s. The "3.6 ft/s" choice scaled by the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio. The "0.45 ft/s" choice inverted the area ratio, treating the smaller pipe as slower. The "1.8 ft/s" choice assumed velocity stays the same because flow is constant.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional operator partly closes the discharge valve on a centrifugal pump. The pump curve does not change. The operating point moves toward:
choices: Lower flow and higher head, because system friction has risen
Higher flow and lower head, because system friction has risen
Lower flow and lower head, because the pump has become weaker
Higher flow and higher head, because the pump runs harder
finalAssessment.explanation: Throttling steepens the system curve, so it crosses the unchanged pump curve at lower flow and higher head. The "Higher flow and lower head, because system friction has risen" choice reverses the shift along the pump curve, since higher friction cannot raise flow. The "Lower flow and lower head, because the pump has become weaker" choice blames the pump curve, which did not change. The "Higher flow and higher head, because the pump runs harder" choice assumes the pump adds energy, when the valve only changes the system curve.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional centrifugal pump shows very high power draw while it delivers far more flow than its design flow. The most likely cause is:
choices: The pump is running near shutoff, with the discharge nearly closed
The pump is running far out on its curve, with the discharge too open
The suction is drawing air, so the pump moves little water
The pump speed has been cut by a variable-speed drive
finalAssessment.explanation: For many centrifugal pumps, power rises as the pump runs out on its curve to high flow, so a very open discharge can overload the motor; the pump's power curve confirms it. The "The pump is running near shutoff, with the discharge nearly closed" choice reverses the effect, since a nearly closed discharge usually lowers power draw. The "The suction is drawing air, so the pump moves little water" choice links air binding to high power, though it usually lowers motor current. The "The pump speed has been cut by a variable-speed drive" choice links a lower speed to higher power, though power falls with speed.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional hydrant flow test shows static pressure of 68 psi and residual pressure of 41 psi at the observation hydrant. Using 2.31 ft per psi, the head consumed by the test flow is:
finalAssessment.explanation: The drop is 68 - 41 = 27 psi, and 27 x 2.31 = 62.4 ft. The "27.0 ft" choice forgot to convert the psi drop into feet of head. The "157.1 ft" choice converted only the static reading, which is the static pressure head and not the drop. The "94.7 ft" choice converted only the residual reading, which is the head left and not the head consumed.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional well pump delivers 1,800 gpm. Using 449 gpm per cfs (1 cfs = 28.3 L/s), the flow in cfs is:
finalAssessment.explanation: 1800 / 449 = 4.01 cfs. The "808,200 cfs" choice multiplied by 449 instead of dividing, so the conversion went the wrong way. The "240.6 cfs" choice divided gallons by 7.48 and stopped, leaving cubic feet per minute. The "30.0 cfs" choice divided by 60 only, which gives gallons per second.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump makes 80 ft of head at 1,750 rpm. Using the affinity law that head varies with the square of speed, the head at 1,400 rpm with the same impeller is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Speed ratio = 1400/1750 = 0.80, and head = 80 x 0.80 squared = 51.2 ft. The "64.0 ft" choice scaled head in direct proportion to speed, which is the flow law. The "41.0 ft" choice cubed the speed ratio, which is the power law. The "125.0 ft" choice inverted the speed ratio and raised head when speed was cut.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional tank is 25 ft in diameter. With no inflow, its level falls 3.5 ft in 6 hours. Using 7.48 gal per ft3, the average demand is about:
finalAssessment.explanation: Area = 490.9 ft2, volume = 1718.1 ft3 = 12,851 gal over 360 min is 35.7 gpm. The "214 gpm" choice divided by 60 instead of the number of minutes in six hours. The "142.8 gpm" choice used the diameter as the radius when finding tank area. The "4.8 gpm" choice forgot to convert cubic feet to gallons with 7.48.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump suction gauge reads 4 psi of vacuum, written as -4 psi (gauge). Taking atmospheric pressure as 14.7 psi (101.3 kPa), the absolute suction pressure is:
finalAssessment.explanation: Absolute equals gauge plus atmospheric: -4 + 14.7 = 10.7 psi, which is below atmospheric. The "18.7 psi" choice added the vacuum reading to atmospheric pressure, which treats the vacuum as positive pressure. The "4.0 psi" choice dropped atmospheric pressure and reported only the size of the vacuum reading. The "14.7 psi" choice ignored the vacuum reading and reported atmospheric pressure alone.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional rectangular channel is 3 ft wide with water 0.8 ft deep, carrying 3.6 cfs. The average velocity is:
finalAssessment.explanation: A = 3 x 0.8 = 2.4 ft2 and V = Q / A = 3.6 / 2.4 = 1.50 ft/s. The "0.67 ft/s" choice inverted the equation and divided area by flow. The "8.64 ft/s" choice multiplied flow by area instead of dividing. The "4.50 ft/s" choice divided by depth alone and left the channel width out of the area.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump delivers 1,000 gpm at 90 ft total head, pump efficiency 70 percent, motor efficiency 92 percent, and runs 8,760 h per year. Using WHP = Q x H / 3,960, BHP = WHP / pump efficiency, input hp = BHP / motor efficiency and 0.746 kW per hp, the yearly energy is about:
finalAssessment.explanation: WHP = 22.73, BHP = 32.47, input = 35.29 hp = 26.33 kW, and x 8760 h = 230,624 kWh. The "148,522 kWh" choice left out both efficiencies, using water horsepower as the power drawn. The "309,147 kWh" choice forgot to convert horsepower to kW with 0.746. The "95,648 kWh" choice multiplied by the efficiencies instead of dividing by them.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant moves a thick, abrasive sludge at a fixed rate with little change in flow as discharge pressure varies. The pump type best matching this is:
choices: A centrifugal pump, which moves less flow as head rises
A positive displacement pump, which moves a fixed volume per stroke or turn
A centrifugal pump, which spins an impeller at high speed
A kinetic pump, which turns water speed into pressure
finalAssessment.explanation: Positive displacement pumps trap a fixed volume each stroke or turn, so flow stays nearly constant while pressure varies. The "A centrifugal pump, which moves less flow as head rises" choice names a kinetic pump whose flow follows the system head along its curve. The "A centrifugal pump, which spins an impeller at high speed" choice names a kinetic pump, which does not hold a fixed rate against varying head. The "A kinetic pump, which turns water speed into pressure" choice names the pump class that includes centrifugal pumps, whose flow changes with head.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional ground-level reservoir has water 95 ft deep over its outlet gauge. Using 0.433 psi per ft (9.79 kPa per m), the static pressure at the gauge is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 95 x 0.433 = 41.13 psi, about 41.1 psi. The "219.5 psi" choice multiplied by 2.31, which moves the answer in the wrong direction for feet to psi. The "55.8 psi" choice added atmospheric pressure to a gauge reading. The "95.4 psi" choice added the constant to the depth instead of multiplying.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Water moves at an average 3 ft/s in a fictional 8 in pipe flowing full (area 0.3491 ft2). Using 449 gpm per cfs (1 cfs = 28.3 L/s), the flow in gpm is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Q = 0.3491 x 3 = 1.047 cfs and x 449 = 470 gpm. The "1.05 gpm" choice stopped at cfs and never converted to gpm. The "1,881 gpm" choice used a diameter-as-radius area of 1.396 ft2. The "0.0023 gpm" choice divided by 449 instead of multiplying.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump draws 30 BHP at 1,750 rpm. Using the affinity law that power varies with the cube of speed, the BHP at 1,400 rpm with the same impeller is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Speed ratio = 0.80, and power = 30 x 0.80 cubed = 15.36 BHP. The "24.0 BHP" choice scaled power in direct proportion to speed, which is the flow law. The "19.2 BHP" choice squared the speed ratio, which is the head law. The "58.6 BHP" choice inverted the speed ratio, which raises power when speed was cut.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional cylindrical tank is 50 ft in diameter. The net inflow is 1,200 gpm. Using 7.48 gal per ft3, the time for the level to rise 4 ft is about:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Area = 1963.5 ft2, volume = 7854.0 ft3 = 58,748 gal, and 58,748 / 1200 = 49.0 min. The "6.5 minutes" choice forgot to convert cubic feet to gallons with 7.48. The "195.8 minutes" choice used the diameter as the radius when finding tank area. The "0.82 minutes" choice divided by 60 and kept the minutes label, which gives hours.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional customer reports a steady 30 psi at a service tap. Using 2.31 ft per psi (0.704 m per psi), the same pressure expressed as head is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 30 x 2.31 = 69.3 ft of head. The "13.0 ft" choice multiplied by 0.433, so feet and psi were swapped. The "206.8 ft" choice used 6.895, the kPa-per-psi constant, and called the answer feet. The "32.3 ft" choice added the constant instead of multiplying.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant averages 5.6 MGD. Using 1 MGD = 1,000,000 gal per day, 1,440 min per day and 1 MGD = 43.8 L/s, the flow in gpm is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 5.6 x 1,000,000 / 1,440 = 3,889 gpm. The "8,064 gpm" choice multiplied 5.6 by 1,440, skipping the million-gallon step and multiplying where a per-day to per-minute conversion divides. The "233,333 gpm" choice divided by 24 only, which gives gallons per hour. The "8.66 gpm" choice used the cfs-per-MGD constant, so the answer is cfs and not gpm.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump takes water from a tank whose surface is 6 ft above the pump centerline and delivers to a tank surface 54 ft above the centerline. Ignoring friction, the static head used in total dynamic head is:
choices: 60 ft, adding the suction head to the discharge head
54 ft, using the discharge head alone
48 ft, the discharge head less the suction head
6 ft, using the suction head alone
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: With a flooded suction the supply helps, so static head = 54 - 6 = 48 ft. The "60 ft" choice adds the suction head, which is correct for a lift but wrong for suction head. The "54 ft" choice ignores the supply side. The "6 ft" choice uses the wrong end of the system.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional centrifugal pump ran normally, then shows almost no flow, a discharge gauge near zero, lower motor current and gurgling at the suction. The best match is:
choices: Water hammer, with the check valve slamming shut
Cavitation, with vapour bubbles collapsing at the impeller
A closed discharge valve, with the pump at shutoff
Lost prime, with air displacing liquid in the casing
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Almost no flow, a near-zero discharge gauge, low current and gurgling fit a pump that has lost prime. The "Water hammer" choice describes a spike with banging, not a quiet loss of flow. The "Cavitation" choice brings gravel noise, vibration and pitting; it does not by itself explain a gauge near zero with lower motor current. The "closed discharge valve" choice would show high pressure near shutoff head, not a gauge near zero.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional standpipe holds water 30 ft deep with no flow. Using 0.433 psi per ft and 2.31 ft per psi, the hydrostatic gauge pressure at its base is:
choices: 69.3 psi, using 2.31 in the wrong direction
27.7 psi, with atmospheric pressure added to the gauge value
0 psi, because the water is not moving
13.0 psi, depth times 0.433 psi per ft
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 30 ft x 0.433 psi per ft = 13.0 psi (12.99 unrounded). The "69.3 psi" choice multiplies by 2.31, which converts the wrong way. The "27.7 psi" choice adds 14.7 psi, which turns a gauge value into an absolute one. The "0 psi" choice confuses rest with zero pressure, because standing water still presses on the base with its depth.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: For steady flow through a fictional pipe that changes diameter, the continuity relationship says that:
choices: Velocity is the same at both sections, so flow is higher where area is larger
Flow is the same at both sections, so velocity is higher where area is smaller
Flow is higher where the pipe is narrower, because the water is squeezed
Pressure is the same at both sections, so the pipe size does not matter
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Steady flow means Q = A1 x V1 = A2 x V2, so a smaller area must carry water at a higher velocity. The "Velocity is the same at both sections, so flow is higher where area is larger" choice assumes velocity stays fixed and lets flow change, the reverse of steady flow. The "Flow is higher where the pipe is narrower, because the water is squeezed" choice confuses a higher velocity with a higher flow. The "Pressure is the same at both sections, so the pipe size does not matter" choice mixes up pressure with flow and ignores area.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump delivers 900 gpm at 55 ft of total head with an efficiency of 65 percent. Using WHP = Q x H / 3,960 and BHP = WHP / efficiency, the brake horsepower is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: WHP = 900 x 55 / 3,960 = 12.50 hp and BHP = 12.50 / 0.65 = 19.23 hp. The "8.1 hp" choice multiplied water horsepower by efficiency instead of dividing. The "12.5 hp" choice stopped at water horsepower and left out the efficiency. The "76,154 hp" choice divided by efficiency but forgot to divide by 3,960.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional crew wants to set the level at which liquid leaves a basin by raising or lowering a sliding pipe sleeve. Which valve type fits?
choices: Mud valve, set in the basin floor to drain settled solids
Pinch valve, a flexible sleeve squeezed shut across the line
Telescoping valve, a sliding sleeve that sets the draw-off level
Plug valve, a quarter-turn plug used to switch sludge lines
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A telescoping valve is a sliding sleeve over a pipe, so raising or lowering it sets where liquid is drawn off. The "Mud valve" choice drains solids from the floor and has no adjustable draw-off level. The "Pinch valve" choice squeezes a sleeve across a line and does not set a level in a basin. The "Plug valve" choice switches or isolates sludge lines with a quarter turn.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional metric tank has water 12 m deep over a gauge. Using 9.79 kPa per m and 101.3 kPa for atmosphere, the gauge pressure is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 12 x 9.79 = 117.5 kPa gauge. The "218.8 kPa" choice added atmospheric pressure to a gauge reading, which gives absolute pressure. The "1.2 kPa" choice divided depth by the constant instead of multiplying. The "17.0 kPa" choice converted the depth to psi (12 m is 39.4 ft, x 0.433 = 17.0 psi) and labelled the result kPa.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Water 0.5 ft deep moves at an average 3 ft/s in a fictional rectangular channel 2 ft wide. Using 449 gpm per cfs, the flow in gpm is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A = 2 x 0.5 = 1.0 ft2, Q = 1.0 x 3 = 3.0 cfs, and x 449 = 1,347 gpm. The "3.0 gpm" choice stopped at the flow in cfs and never converted to gpm. The "22.4 gpm" choice multiplied by 7.48 only, which gives gallons per second. The "0.007 gpm" choice divided by 449 instead of multiplying.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional pump delivers 1,000 gpm with pump efficiency 70 percent and motor efficiency 92 percent, running 8,760 h per year. Using WHP = Q x H / 3,960, BHP = WHP / pump efficiency, input hp = BHP / motor efficiency and 0.746 kW per hp, one extra foot of head costs about this much energy per year:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Per foot: 1000 x 1 / 3,960 = 0.2525 WHP, / 0.7 / 0.92 = 0.3921 hp, x 0.746 = 0.2925 kW, x 8,760 = 2,562 kWh. The "1,650 kWh" choice left out both efficiencies. The "3,435 kWh" choice forgot to convert hp to kW with 0.746. The "2,357 kWh" choice divided by pump efficiency but left out motor efficiency.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional crew wants to hold a line at a steady partial flow for several weeks. Which valve choice suits that duty?
choices: A gate valve, because it seals tightly when fully closed
A check valve, because it passes flow in one direction
A knife gate valve, because its blade cuts through solids
A globe valve, because it is built to operate partly open
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Globe valves are made to sit partly open, while gate and knife gate valves are for isolation and are not meant for throttling. The "A gate valve, because it seals tightly when fully closed" choice uses an isolation valve for throttling, which can damage its gate and seat. The "A check valve, because it passes flow in one direction" choice uses a self-acting valve for control, which gives no adjustable flow. The "A knife gate valve, because its blade cuts through solids" choice uses an isolation valve for throttling, since it is meant to be open or closed.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: In a fictional distribution zone, residual pressure during a large draw is lower than static pressure at the same hydrant. The main reason is:
choices: Energy is lost to friction while the water is moving through the pipes
The water in the zone weighs less once it begins to flow
Atmospheric pressure drops when the hydrant valve is opened
The gauge shows absolute pressure rather than gauge pressure
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Moving water spends head on friction and fittings, so the pressure remaining while flowing is lower than the static value. The "The water in the zone weighs less once it begins to flow" choice assumes flow changes the weight of water, which does not happen. The "Atmospheric pressure drops when the hydrant valve is opened" choice assumes opening a hydrant changes the air pressure around it, which it does not in any meaningful way. The "The gauge shows absolute pressure rather than gauge pressure" choice mixes up the zero reference with a flow effect.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional 6 in pipe carries 400 gpm. Using 449 gpm per cfs and a full-pipe area of 0.1963 ft2, the velocity is:
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: 400 / 449 = 0.8909 cfs and V = 0.8909 / 0.1963 = 4.54 ft/s. The "2,037 ft/s" choice skipped the conversion from gpm to cfs. The "1.13 ft/s" choice used a diameter-as-radius area of 0.785 ft2 for the division. The "0.17 ft/s" choice multiplied flow by area instead of dividing.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional centrifugal pump with a typical falling curve has a shutoff head, its highest head, of 90 ft, and the discharge point is 105 ft above the water source. At the pump, the result is:
choices: No flow, because the pump cannot overcome the static head
Reduced flow, because the pump works against the extra 15 ft
Full flow, because water always follows the pump curve
Higher flow, because a higher static head raises the pump curve
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: On this falling curve, shutoff head is the most head the pump can produce. If static head is above it, the pump cannot move water to the discharge. The "Reduced flow, because the pump works against the extra 15 ft" choice assumes some flow can occur when the pump cannot lift to the discharge. The "Full flow, because water always follows the pump curve" choice ignores that the pump must be able to exceed the static head before any water reaches the discharge. The "Higher flow, because a higher static head raises the pump curve" choice assumes static head changes the pump curve, when it only changes the system curve.
